title: Lady Mary and Onesimus
summary: A brave English writer saw women in Turkey protecting children from smallpox, and she brought the idea home to London. Across the ocean in Boston, an enslaved African man named Onesimus explained the very same trick. Together, their knowledge sparked a huge argument, and a few bold experiments.

sections.heading: A Face Changed Forever
paragraphs: In December 1715, in a grand house in London, a 26-year-old woman lay in bed with a burning fever. Her name was Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, and she was one of the cleverest, sharpest and most talked-about people in English high society. She wrote poems, sparkling letters and funny, sometimes cutting, verses about the royal court. She had taught herself Latin as a girl by sneaking into her father's library, at a time when most people thought girls did not need to learn such things. Now she had smallpox.

Lady Mary knew exactly how dangerous that was. Two years earlier, in 1713, her younger brother had died of the same disease. As her illness went on, the fever was followed by the rash of bumps that gave smallpox its name, spreading across her face and body. For days nobody could be sure whether she would live.

She survived. But the disease left its mark. Her smooth skin was left pitted with small scars, and she lost her eyelashes, which never grew back. In the 1700s, a beautiful complexion was considered one of a noblewoman's most valuable features, and many people in her circle would have seen her scars as a terrible loss. Lady Mary was too tough and too clever to hide away, but she never forgot what smallpox had done to her family and to her face.

While she was still recovering, there was more trouble. Some of her private satirical poems, called the 'court eclogues', were passed around and gossiped about. One of them was read by many as poking fun at Caroline, Princess of Wales, the wife of the heir to the throne. This is worth remembering, because just a few years later Lady Mary and Princess Caroline would end up on the same side of a very important argument.

Lady Mary was married to Edward Wortley Montagu, a politician. The couple had run away together to marry in 1712 because her father disapproved of the match. They had a small son, also called Edward, born in 1713. Within a year of Lady Mary's illness, the whole family would be packing their trunks for one of the most extraordinary journeys any English family made in that age.

sections.heading: Engrafting in Constantinople
paragraphs: In 1716, Edward Wortley Montagu was appointed British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire, the vast realm ruled by the Sultan from Constantinople (today's Istanbul, in Turkey). His job was to help negotiate peace in a war between the Ottomans and Austria. In August 1716 the family set off overland, travelling through Vienna and across central Europe and the Balkans, through snowy mountains and along muddy roads, to the Ottoman city of Adrianople (now Edirne) and then on to Constantinople. The journey took months.

Lady Mary was fascinated by everything she saw. She visited Turkish bathhouses where women met and talked, learned some Turkish, wore Ottoman clothes, and wrote long, lively letters home describing daily life. Those letters were later published as the 'Turkish Embassy Letters' and are still read today. One of them, dated 1 April 1717 and written to a friend in England, became famous for a completely different reason. It described smallpox.

In her letter, Lady Mary explained that smallpox, so deadly in England, was made almost harmless in Turkey by a practice she called 'engrafting', the same thing we call variolation or inoculation. Every autumn, she wrote, in September when the great heat was over, families would arrange gatherings so that children could be engrafted together. An old woman would arrive carrying a nutshell full of material from the sores of someone with a mild case of smallpox. She would open a small scratch in the skin with a needle, put in as much of the matter as would fit on the needle's tip, and bind up the little wound with a piece of shell.

According to Lady Mary's description, the children then played as normal for about eight days. After that a fever came, they stayed in bed for a couple of days, and they usually had only a few spots on the face, which did not leave scars. In about eight more days they were well again. She wrote that thousands of people underwent the operation every year and that she had never heard of anyone dying of it. That was surely too rosy a picture, because we know variolation could kill about 1 or 2 in every 100 people. But compared with natural smallpox, which killed about 30 in every 100 people who caught the deadly form, it was a very good bargain.

Lady Mary was not the first person to tell the English about this practice. A few years earlier, two doctors working in the region, Emanuel Timoni and Giacomo Pylarini, had sent letters describing Ottoman inoculation to the Royal Society in London. Timoni's account was printed in the Society's journal, the Philosophical Transactions, in 1714, and Pylarini's followed in 1716. Members found the reports interesting, but nobody in England actually tried the method. It sounded like a strange foreign folk custom. What made Lady Mary different was that she decided to test it on someone she loved.

In March 1718, she had her son Edward, then nearly five years old, inoculated at the British Embassy. The embassy surgeon, a Scotsman named Charles Maitland, supervised. By the accounts of the time, an elderly local woman who was an experienced inoculator began the operation on one arm, and Maitland himself did the other arm. Little Edward developed a mild illness, recovered, and was protected for life. He is usually described as the first English person to undergo the operation.

Imagine how Lady Mary felt during those days of waiting. She was taking a calculated risk with her own child, based on what she had seen with her own eyes and on the experience of thousands of Ottoman families. Her husband was away at the time, and she wrote to him about the boy's progress. It went well. She was now convinced that inoculation could save English children, and she promised herself she would bring it home. The family returned to London on 2 October 1718.

sections.heading: Back in London: A Daughter and an Epidemic
paragraphs: For a little while, nothing much happened. Lady Mary talked about inoculation, but English doctors were not interested in learning a medical technique from Turkish village women, and certainly not from an aristocratic lady who was not a physician. Many doctors also earned good money treating smallpox patients, and some suspected that the whole idea was dangerous nonsense.

Then, in 1721, a serious smallpox epidemic hit London. People were dying across the city, and families were frightened. Lady Mary had a little daughter, also named Mary, who was about three years old and had been born in Constantinople. She had not been inoculated there because she was then too young. Now, with smallpox all around, Lady Mary decided it was time.

Charles Maitland had returned to England too. Lady Mary asked him to inoculate her daughter. He was nervous about doing it in London, where a bad result could ruin his reputation, so he insisted that other doctors be present as witnesses. In April 1721, Maitland carried out the operation. It was the first inoculation known to have been performed in England by a trained surgeon in front of witnesses.

The little girl came through her mild case of smallpox safely. Lady Mary invited important visitors to see her, including Sir Hans Sloane, physician to the King and one of the most famous doctors and collectors in Britain (his collection later helped found the British Museum). Several doctors came to look at the child, and word spread quickly through the city's drawing rooms, coffee houses and newspapers.

From then on, Lady Mary became inoculation's most energetic champion in England. She told everyone she met about it, encouraged her friends to inoculate their children, and later wrote about it in print. In September 1722 she published an article arguing for inoculation in a London newspaper. She did not sign it with her own name. Instead she pretended to be 'a Turkey Merchant', perhaps because people might take a merchant's opinion more seriously than a woman's. In her article she also argued that some English doctors were making the operation more dangerous by cutting too deeply and adding needless treatments.

Not everyone thanked her. Some doctors and clergymen attacked inoculation as unnatural, risky or even sinful. In their view, giving a healthy person a disease on purpose was interfering with the will of God. Lady Mary later wrote that she was criticised and even blamed whenever an inoculated child became ill. But she had something powerful on her side: two healthy children who had both had smallpox on purpose and both lived.

sections.heading: The Royal Experiment at Newgate
paragraphs: Two healthy children were encouraging, but doctors and the royal family wanted more proof. Was inoculation truly safe? And did it really protect people for life, or did it only seem to? To find out, the authorities arranged a test that we would find shocking today.

Newgate was London's most notorious prison, a dark, crowded building near the old city wall where people convicted of serious crimes waited to be hanged. In the summer of 1721, prisoners there who had been sentenced to death were offered a deal. If they agreed to be inoculated with smallpox, and if they survived, they would be pardoned and set free. The King, George I, gave his permission, and the plan was supported by Caroline, Princess of Wales, who was very interested in the results.

On 9 August 1721, Charles Maitland inoculated six prisoners, three men and three women, in front of a crowd of doctors and scientists who came to watch. (Some accounts say seven prisoners were offered the chance; the usual figure for those inoculated is six.) Maitland made small cuts in their arms and legs and placed smallpox material into them. Then everyone waited, and the witnesses visited to record what happened.

Five of the six developed mild smallpox and recovered. One man did not seem to react much at all, and it was later suggested that he had already had smallpox earlier in life, which would have made him immune. All six survived, and all six were released, as promised. Newspapers followed the story eagerly.

The doctors wanted one more piece of evidence. Were the prisoners truly protected? One of the women, Elizabeth Harrison, was sent to the town of Hertford, where smallpox was spreading. There she was asked to nurse a sick child and even to sleep in the same bed as a boy with smallpox. She did not catch the disease. To the doctors, this showed that the protection was real.

It is important to say clearly that an experiment like this would never be allowed today. The prisoners were facing execution, so they could hardly make a free choice; saying no meant the gallows. Nobody explained the risks in the careful, honest way that modern rules require, and Elizabeth Harrison was deliberately exposed to a deadly disease. Today, medical research must follow strict ethical rules: volunteers must give 'informed consent', which means they understand the risks and agree freely, and vulnerable people such as prisoners are given special protection. Those rules were written partly because of experiments like this one, and because of much worse abuses in later centuries.

Still, in the eyes of people in 1721, the 'Royal Experiment' was a success. It was one of the earliest attempts in Britain to test a medical procedure on a group of people and watch the results, rather than just relying on old books or opinions.

sections.heading: A Princess Makes It Fashionable
paragraphs: Caroline of Ansbach, Princess of Wales, was a thoughtful, well-read woman who loved science and philosophy. She also had a very personal reason to care about smallpox: she had survived it herself in 1707, and she had young daughters. If inoculation worked, it could protect her children, and they were important members of the royal family who might one day marry into other royal houses across Europe.

But she wanted to be sure. After the Newgate trial, a second test was arranged. In early 1722 several orphan children from the parish of St James's in London were inoculated. Like the prisoners, they all survived. Once again, the children had no real say in the matter, which modern ethics would not accept.

Finally, in April 1722, the princess's two daughters, Princess Amelia, aged 10, and Princess Caroline, aged 8, were inoculated. The operation was performed by Claudius Amyand, a French-born royal surgeon, with Charles Maitland's help. Both girls had mild cases and recovered completely.

In the 1700s, whatever the royal family did quickly became fashionable among the rich. Once the princesses had been inoculated, many aristocratic families wanted the same protection for their own children. Inoculation went from being a strange foreign custom to something talked about in the finest homes in London. Lady Mary, whose poem had once seemed to mock the princess, now found Caroline a powerful ally.

The arguments did not stop, though. In July 1722 a clergyman named Edmund Massey preached a famous sermon in London attacking 'the dangerous and sinful practice of inoculation'. He argued that diseases were sent by God, either to test people or to punish them, and that humans had no right to give them to themselves. Other critics pointed to real problems. A few inoculated people died. And, worst of all, inoculated people had a genuine case of smallpox, so they could pass the full, deadly disease on to anyone around them who was not immune.

To settle the argument with facts, a doctor and mathematician named James Jurin, secretary of the Royal Society, began collecting numbers in the 1720s. He gathered reports of as many inoculations and natural smallpox cases as he could find. His figures suggested that roughly 1 in 50 inoculated people died, while somewhere around 1 in 6 or 7 people who caught smallpox naturally died. Counting and comparing like this was a new way of answering a medical question, and it would become one of the most important tools in all of medicine.

sections.heading: Onesimus: Knowledge From Africa
paragraphs: Now we must cross the Atlantic Ocean and go back a few years, to the busy port town of Boston in the British colony of Massachusetts. Boston in the early 1700s had about 11,000 people, wooden houses, wharves crowded with ships, and many churches. It was also a place where slavery was legal. Around a thousand or so of its people were enslaved Africans or their descendants.

In December 1706, the members of Boston's North Church gave an enslaved young man as a 'gift' to their minister, Cotton Mather. Mather was one of the most famous preachers in New England, a man who wrote hundreds of books and pamphlets and was deeply interested in science. He renamed the young man Onesimus, after an enslaved man mentioned in the Bible. We do not know the name Onesimus was given by his own family, and we know only a little about his life, mostly from what Mather wrote. He came from West Africa, probably from a region where people spoke languages of the Akan family, though historians are not completely certain.

One day Mather asked Onesimus whether he had ever had smallpox. Onesimus's answer was surprising: both yes and no. He explained that, as a child in Africa, he had undergone an operation that gave him something of the smallpox and protected him from it forever. He showed Mather the scar on his arm. As Mather later reported it, Onesimus described how people took material from smallpox sores, cut the skin, and put in a drop. This was the same basic idea that Lady Mary would see in Constantinople, practised thousands of kilometres away.

Mather was curious enough to ask other Africans living in Boston, and he wrote that several of them described the same practice and said it was common in their homelands. Then, by 1716, he had read Emanuel Timoni's report of Ottoman inoculation in the Philosophical Transactions. Two completely different sources, one from Africa and one from the Ottoman Empire, described the same method. In 1716 Mather wrote a letter to the Royal Society in London describing what Onesimus had told him and saying that, if smallpox ever came to Boston again, he would push for inoculation.

Onesimus's story shows something important about the history of science. Ideas do not only come from famous people in universities and laboratories. African healers had developed and passed down inoculation over many generations, and an enslaved man carried that knowledge in his memory across an ocean. Yet when Mather later promoted inoculation, many people in Boston mocked him for trusting the word of an enslaved African, a sign of the prejudice of the time.

We know that in 1716 Onesimus tried to buy his freedom. He raised money so that Mather could buy another enslaved young man to replace him, and Mather agreed under certain conditions, including that Onesimus would still come and work for the household when needed. Records of what happened to him afterwards are very thin. But his knowledge was about to save lives.

sections.heading: Boston 1721: Fear, Fury and Figures
paragraphs: On 22 April 1721, a merchant ship called the Seahorse sailed into Boston harbour from the West Indies. On board were sailors sick with smallpox. Boston had not had a big smallpox epidemic for almost twenty years, which meant that a whole generation of young people had never had the disease and were not immune. By late May, Cotton Mather was writing in his diary that smallpox had entered the town. Soon the disease was spreading from house to house.

Cotton Mather remembered Onesimus. In June 1721 he wrote to Boston's doctors, urging them to try inoculation. Almost all of them refused. Only one answered his call: Zabdiel Boylston, a 42-year-old physician who had trained by apprenticeship rather than at a university.

On 26 June 1721, Boylston inoculated three people: his own six-year-old son Thomas, and two enslaved people he owned, a man named Jack, aged 36, and Jack's two-year-old son, Jackey. He used a method like the one Onesimus had described, putting matter from a smallpox sore into small cuts in the skin. Like Newgate, the choice of enslaved people as some of the first test subjects is something that modern ethics would condemn, since they had no power to refuse. All three recovered.

Boylston carried on, and over the following months he inoculated more and more people. Many Bostonians were furious. The town's best-educated doctor, William Douglass, who had a medical degree from Europe, attacked inoculation as reckless and said ministers should leave medicine to physicians. A newspaper called the New-England Courant, run by James Franklin (the older brother of the young Benjamin Franklin, who worked in the print shop), printed articles against it. Town officials tried to stop Boylston, and he faced threats so serious that, by one account, he hid for 14 days and visited his patients only at midnight, in disguise.

The anger reached a frightening peak in November 1721. In the middle of the night, someone threw a lit grenade, a small bomb, through the window of Cotton Mather's house, into the room where a relative who had just been inoculated was staying. Luckily it did not explode; according to the story usually told, its fuse was knocked off as it smashed through the glass. Tied to it was a note full of angry threats against Mather. Nobody was hurt, but the attack showed how bitterly divided the town had become.

The epidemic peaked in October 1721, when 411 people died in a single month. By the time it was over, the town recorded 5,889 people who had caught smallpox naturally, and 844 of them had died. That is about 14 in every 100, or roughly one in seven.

Boylston, meanwhile, kept careful records. Accounts give slightly different totals, but he inoculated roughly 240 to 290 people during the epidemic, and only six of them died. That is about 2 in every 100. Even allowing for the fact that his patients may have been healthier on average, the difference was dramatic: natural smallpox was about seven times more deadly than inoculation.

This comparison is one of the earliest examples of using numbers from two groups of people to judge whether a medical treatment works. In 1724 Boylston travelled to London, carrying a letter of introduction from Mather to James Jurin, and published his results as 'An Historical Account of the Small-Pox Inoculated in New England'. In 1726 he was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society, one of the first people from the American colonies to receive that honour.

By 1722, then, inoculation had a foothold on both sides of the Atlantic. A noblewoman, a princess, a Scottish surgeon, an enslaved African, a Puritan minister and a stubborn Boston doctor had all played a part. But the story was far from over. Inoculation was still risky, killing roughly one or two people in every hundred. It was expensive, with weeks of illness and care. It could start new outbreaks. And it was fiercely controversial. Over the next seventy years, it would spread to empresses and armies, but it would remain a dangerous gamble.

deepDive: Historians see the inoculation debates of 1721 and 1722 as a turning point in how medicine decided what works. Before this, doctors relied mostly on ancient authorities such as Galen and on personal experience. The inoculation arguments pushed people to count. Boylston's Boston figures (about 2 percent of inoculated people dying versus about 14 percent of natural cases, out of 5,889 natural infections and 844 deaths) and James Jurin's yearly reports for the Royal Society, which compared roughly 1 death in 50 inoculations with roughly 1 in 6 or 7 natural cases, are among the earliest uses of comparative numbers to judge a medical practice. They were not modern clinical trials. There was no random assignment and no control for age or health, and the people who chose inoculation may have been richer, better fed and less exposed. Modern scholars also point out that such records missed people who caught smallpox from inoculated patients, a real cost that was hard to count. Even so, these early tallies changed the shape of the argument from a clash of opinions into a question that evidence could answer. Another debate is about credit. Older histories often told this story as if English doctors and Lady Mary simply 'discovered' inoculation. Historians now stress that the knowledge came from women healers in the Ottoman world and from African communities, with Onesimus as the best-documented messenger. The prejudice Mather faced for trusting an enslaved man, and the use of prisoners, orphans and enslaved people as early test subjects, are now studied as part of the history of medical ethics. These episodes help explain why modern research demands informed consent and special protection for vulnerable groups. Finally, historians note that the Newgate prisoners' 'success' proved less than it seemed. Six people is a tiny sample, and one of them was probably already immune. The real persuasive power came from the growing pile of numbers over the following years.
funFact: Cotton Mather, the Boston minister who championed inoculation in 1721, learned about it partly from Onesimus, and the grenade thrown into his house that November failed to explode, reportedly because its fuse was knocked off as it crashed through the window.

check.q: In Boston in 1721, roughly what share of inoculated people died, compared with people who caught smallpox naturally?
check.a: About 2 in 100 inoculated people died, compared with about 14 in 100 natural cases
wrong: About 30 in 100 inoculated people died, compared with about 2 in 100 natural cases
